<reflection>
- The first experiment resulted in very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values across all 20 models (ranging from -25.6 to -23.1). This indicates that under standard, moderate conditions without initial product, the models can fit the data almost equally well by adjusting their respective rate constants.
- The aim of establishing a baseline was achieved, but as expected, a single moderate condition is insufficient to strongly separate the models. We must now perturb the system into a regime where the divergent mechanistic features (higher-order dependencies and product effects) dominate.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To force the models to diverge, we need to amplify the non-linear and product-dependent terms in the candidate mechanisms. 
1. By setting the initial product concentration to its maximum allowed value (0.5), models with product-induced deactivation (M12, M17) will exhibit immediate and strong suppression of the reaction rate right from t=0, distinguishing them from models where product is inert.
2. By increasing the catalyst concentration to its maximum (0.20), models with second-order catalyst dependencies (such as dimerization in M2, M3, or bimolecular deactivation in M13, M18, M19) will show drastically different kinetic profiles compared to strictly first-order catalyst models. The rate of these second-order processes will increase by a factor of 16 compared to the first experiment (0.20^2 / 0.05^2).
3. By increasing the substrate concentration to 4.0, we will amplify substrate-induced deactivation (M11, M16) and higher-order substrate kinetics (M7). 
This combination of high S, high cat, and high P will simultaneously probe multiple distinct mechanistic features, leading to a broad and informative separation of the candidate models.
</hypothesis>
